In 2020, Piedmont Unified School District passed a Racial Equity board policy that made Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services Dr. Cheryl Wozniak responsible for its implementation. Dr. Wozniak thought the course grading formula should be standardized keeping a goal of racial equity in mind. Since roughly 2020, some PMS and PHS teachers voluntarily began experimenting with a grading system based on a book called “Grading for Equity” by Joe Feldman. Do racial differences in grade distributions prove a biased education? As school board president, Veronica Andersen Thigpen agendized this topic for action by the board at a public meeting on March 22, 2023, but did not appear at the meeting to defend her position. Thigpen, who is a Fellow at Just Equations, a nonprofit that reconceptualizes the role of math in ensuring educational equity, ran for school board in 2020 on the premise that there should be equity in educational outcomes for all races. At the public meeting on March 22, 2023, Wozniak led a presentation on “Equitable Grading Practices” to update the school board on her efforts with support from PMS and PHS school principals. Wozniak argued: “Teachers sincerely want their students’ grades to be objective, but our grading systems historically have systemically perpetuated opportunity gaps and biases. For example: providing extra credit, penalizing for lateness, punishing cheating in the grade, evaluating student behavior (like how often a student raises their hand and participates), and including homework. These are all biased grading practices and dependent on a student’s life circumstances, culture, and for all kinds of reasons.” Feldman’s grading is solely based on a student’s mastery of the content based on assessments, nothing behavioral. Feldman prohibits grading credit for homework completion, class participation, extra credit, or grade punishment for cheating because it disproportionately impacts low-income and minority students. Instead, he promotes giving students the option to be retested or resubmit work in subject areas the student did not master (a.k.a. Mastery-Based Grading), and instead of a failing grade below 50%, he would give students an incomplete that would not count against their GPA.

articles.text: Although the Corporation Yard by Coaches Field was among the buildings affected by the power outages that swept the city during a heavy rain and windstorm on Tuesday, March 21, a portable backup generator from Alameda County kept it operating with no interruption. Full power was restored on Thursday. “We received [two grants] about $780,000 combined, about two years ago. Each grant was roughly half and with them our office, the Alameda County Office of Emergency Services, purchased seven portable trailered generators,” said Lt. Richard Macintire of the Alameda County “About one year ago,” said Macintire, “County Sheriff’s Office officials conducted site visits to cities interested in having universal generator hookups installed at critical buildings which had no alternative power.” The survey came after the widespread PG&E wildfire and wind damage power shutoffs which Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan was “one of the first among cities in the county to have us come out, get a bid for the job, and have the project awarded,” explained Macintire. “Piedmont was the first to complete the projOther cities receiving generators were Dublin, Emeryville, Hayward, Livermore, and San Leandro, in addition to Alameda “The funding was first come, first served for cities with the hookup installed. While we don’t own the generator, we own that connector. As subgrantees, when the power went out during the storms [on March 21], we called the county and received it the same day,” Brannigan explained. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the city received the generator less than two hours after making the request by phone. Gonzales said that the Corporation Yard was the highest priority for the city as a building not on backup power. “It’s where we keep our fuel, many police and fire vehicles, backup engines, and some heavier equipment like chainsaws. When we lose power there, it’s challenging to get that equipment out for emergency response,” he said. The city’s emergency call dispatch center already has a generator. A portable generator donated by Alameda County will allow the offices at the city’s Corporation Yard to operate without interruption during storms and power outages.
articles.title: City receives backup generator for Corp. Yard offices

articles.text: A time-lapse camera was installed on Monday, April 3, on the roof of the Piedmont Recreation Center to record progress at the Piedmont Community Pool site, with a photo feed available on the city website. Photos will be uploaded to the city website every 15 minutes from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. at piedmont. ca.gov/newpool. Piedmont Communications Manager Echa Schneider confirmed that the cost of camera and installation was $13,500. The online host service is webcam provider EarthCam. Pool excavation continues, but at a slower pace due to the rain between December and March. The contractors have been busy preventing on-site flooding by pumping out water which accumulated in the holes cut in bedrock for the new main and medium-sized pools. However, the biggest storm-related challenge and the main reason for delays has been PG&E. Its utility workers were originally expected to come as soon as Friday, March 10, but they still haven’t arrived to pull meters and disconnect the power from the sites of former pool facility buildings. Construction manager George Sanen reached out to PG&E three times in the last week, but “we still haven’t received a confirmed day,” said Gonzales. “They must be backlogged with more urgent storm damage response tasks and in the meantime the contractors are working to minimize schedule impacts.“ “The biggest impact is because there are still live gas lines, identifying where they are, largely keeping things in place there, and digging slowly elsewhere. Since it’s more about a change in sequence they’re still able to do much of the work. They’re finishing up on moving out concrete and steel; soon it’ll just be soil,” said Gonzales. Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. For questions or comments about parking and traffic, contact Gonzales by email at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont. ca.gov/newpool. A time-lapse camera recently installed at the Community Pool construction site will provide ongoing images of the progress of the city’s new swimming pools.

The bulk of the costs are for third-party contractors assisting in cleanup and additional internal personnel costs (overtime After being pounded by heavy rain and wind on March 21, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the storm one week later on March 28 “paled in comparison to the previous ones. The rain intensity was so spread out, more like a Seattle drizzle than a New Mexico flash flood,” he said. Although Piedmont faced no downed trees or power lines like it did earlier, “Even small amounts of rain at this point create issues that we don’t typically see because the ground is so saturated,” Gonzales added. The primary damage caused by last week’s storm was the creation of a sinkhole at Hampton and Crest Roads. Although it was “fairly small”, roughly 12” square, “it can still ruin the tire and mess up the axle of any vehicle [that] hits it. We’ve been putting cones out and patching it up until PG&E comes to dig a trench and make the repair,” said Gonzales. Workers with the Public Works Department have been patching the sinkhole temporarily with cold patch asphalt. “It’s a fast fix — you open the bag, dump it in, but since it’s not hot, it breaks up faster … [requiring replacement] after a few days if water is involved.” Residents with questions about storm costs can contact Michael Szczech by phone at 420-3045 or by email at mszczech@piedmont.ca.gov. pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 5, 2023 3 By Selen Ozturk Although the Corporation Yard by Coaches Field was among the buildings affected by the power outages that swept the city during a heavy rain and windstorm on Tuesday, March 21, a portable backup generator from Alameda County kept it operating with no interruption. Full power was restored on Thursday. March 23. “We received [two grants] about $780,000 combined, about two years ago. Each grant was roughly half and with them our office, the Alameda County Office of Emergency Services, purchased seven portable trailered generators,” said Lt. Richard Macintire of the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office. “About one year ago,” said Macintire, “County Sheriff’s Office officials conducted site visits to cities interested in having universal generator hookups installed at critical buildings which had no alternative power.” The survey came after the widespread PG&E wildfire and wind damage power shutoffs which began occurring in 2019. Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan was “one of the first among cities in the county to have us come out, get a bid for the job, and have the project awarded,” explained Macintire. “Piedmont was the first to complete the project and use the system.” Other cities receiving generators were Dublin, Emeryville, Hayward, Livermore, and San Leandro, in addition to Alameda County. “The funding was first come, first served for cities with the City receives backup generator for Corp. Yard offices hookup installed. While we don’t own the generator, we own that connector. As subgrantees, when the power went out during the storms [on March 21], we called the county and received it the same day,” Brannigan explained. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the city received the generator less than two hours after making the request by phone. Gonzales said that the Corporation Yard was the highest priority for the city as a building not on backup power. “It’s where we keep our fuel, many police and fire vehicles, backup engines, and some heavier equipment like chainsaws. When we lose power there, it’s challenging to get that equipment out for emergency response,” he said. The city’s emergency call dispatch center already has a generator. A portable generator donated by Alameda County will allow the offices at the city’s Corporation Yard to operate without interruption during storms and power outages. Storms cost city $185,000 so far By Selen Ozturk As the weather which brought so much rain, wind, and even snow to Piedmont and the East Bay Hills melts into spring, city staff continue to assess the damage and residual effects in the city. Piedmont Finance Director Michael Szczech said, “The city has incurred just under $185,000 in costs related to storms since December. The bulk of the costs are for third-party contractors assisting in cleanup and additional internal personnel costs (overtime and related payroll taxes).” After being pounded by heavy rain and wind on March 21, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the storm one week later on March 28 “paled in comparison to the previous ones. The rain intensity was so spread out, more like a Seattle drizzle than a New Mexico flash flood,” he said. Although Piedmont faced no downed trees or power lines like it did earlier, “Even small amounts of rain at this point create issues that we don’t typically see because the ground is so saturated,” Gonzales added. The primary damage caused by last week’s storm was the creation of a sinkhole at Hampton and Crest Roads. Although it was “fairly small”, roughly 12” square, “it can still ruin the tire and mess up the axle of any vehicle [that] hits it. We’ve been putting cones out and patching it up until PG&E comes to dig a trench and make the repair,” said Gonzales. Workers with the Public Works Department have been patching the sinkhole temporarily with cold patch asphalt. “It’s a fast fix — you open the bag, dump it in, but since it’s not hot, it breaks up faster … [requiring replacement] after a few days if water is involved.” Residents with questions about storm costs can contact Michael Szczech by phone at 420-3045 or by email at mszczech@piedmont.ca.gov. Those with questions about storm damage repairs can contact Daniel Gonzales by phone at 420-3061 or by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Salvation Army will hold its eighth annual gala on Sunday, April 30 at 5 p.m. at the University Club in UC Berkeley’s Memorial Stadium. Chaired by Debbie Kelley of Piedmont, the event will feature live music from the UC Berkeley a cappella group DeCadence, live and silent auctions, testimonials from inspiring Salvation Army beneficiaries, and dinner. The Volunteer of the Year honoree Elijah Hicks, will be introduced. A former UC Berkeley football player, he was drafted by the Chicago Bears last year and has chosen the Salvation Army for philanthropy through his foundation, Intercept Poverty. The organization provides financial assistance to low-income students. All proceeds will help fund The Salvation Army’s efforts to meet human need in Alameda County. The non-profit helps with food, rent, and utility assistance, operates a homeless shelter and homeless outreach programs, preschools, after-school programs, a summer camp in the Sierra foothills, music programs, Christmas assistance, and workforce development programs in construction and certified nurse’s assistant training. Kelley, who is chairing the event for her fourth year, has been on the Salvation Army advisory board since 2016. She confirmed that last year’s gala raised over $420,000 with 150 people in attendance. A similar crowd is expected this year. “The people involved before me said they were lucky to clear $100,000,” said Kelley. “Now we clear $300,000-$400,000, much due Corki Recht, the co-chair for three years.” When Kelley was unavailable last year due to an emergency, Recht ran the event, the first time the gala was held at Memorial Stadium, In prior years it had been held at the Claremont Country Club. Wanting a change of venue, Kelley, who works in College Relations at UC Berkeley, approached the school’s Athletics Director, Jim Knowlton, who encouraged the move. “It was then that we decided to honor a Cal student volunteer,” said Kelley. In 2022 the honoree was professional baseball player Tyson Ross, a pitcher who has created a “Loyal to my Soil” program providing baseball lessons to inner-city children. Highlights at this year’s live auction includes a dinner for 10 cooked by Salvation Army Culinary Director Tim Tucker, and a testimonial by Thomas Wolf, a former homeless man and drug addict who has since reinvented his life due to his work with the Salvation Army. “People think of the Salvation Army as red kettles and thrift stores,” said Kelley, “but they provide such important rehabilitation and emergency service work. articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present an evening of Short Films on April 20 at 7:00 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus at 325 Highland Avenue Help the Appreciating Diversity Film Series enrich the Piedmont Food Fest’s celebration of Bay Area diversity with five family friendly films that will explore the many flavors of families. Bring your family and friends and experience the range of family diversity through themes such as adoption, homelessness, women’s issues, education, and gender identity. The films are appropriate for children ages 10 and up. As always, Diversity films are free. The films which will be screened starting at 7:00 p.m. are listed below in the order in which they will be seen. The total running time for all five films is about one hour. • Absolutely No Spitting A Jewish mother and her multiracial 4-year-old adopted daughter explore their DNA profiles and what it means to have many identities and cultures in your genetic heritage. • A Concerto Is a Conversation A virtuoso jazz pianist and film composer traces his family’s lineage through his 91-year-old grandfather from Jim Crow laws in Florida to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. The grandfather describes the development of his love for music as well as his ingenious methods of getting ahead that made it possible for his family to thrive then and for coming generations. • Almost Famous: The Silent Pulse of the Universe In 1967, a young astronomer, Jocelyn Bell, made a breakthrough discovery in astronomy, but as a woman in the sciences her role was overlooked and unfairly ignored. While Jocelyn was belittled and sexually harassed by the media, the Nobel Prize was awarded to her professor and his boss. • What You’ll Remember The story of young Bay Area parents determined to give their four children a good life despite moving in and out of homelessness over a period of fifteen years. While the family waited for stable, affordable housing, they nurtured and educated their children in resourceful, inspiring ways, creating a feeling of “home” even when there was no house. • Texas Strong Kai Shappley, a 6-year old trans child in Texas, fights to be recognized and accepted by her devout Christian family. Kai’s mother, Shirley, must deal with her church, while Kai navigates life at school, where she is banned from the girls’ bathroom. Winner of the 2018 Emmy for Outstanding Short Documentary. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by Piedmont School District, the City of Piedmont, the Oakland and Piedmont Leagues of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee.

articles.text: Photos by Selen Ozturk. Off-season and holiday clothing in a Dress Best for Less storage room. On Tuesday morning, March 21, Dress Best for Less volunteers returned to their marking room at First Congregational Church in Oakland to see that their storage bins, and everything inside them had been destroyed by an arson fire the night before. Some DBFL staff say that the event feels like the tipping point of six months of insecurity since the non-profit thrift business was forced last October from the now-demolished Carriage House, by the Piedmont Pool. DBFL has raised over $1 million dollars for Piedmont School District since its founding in 1982, through sales of donated items to its retail shop on Piedmont Avenue. However, neither the school district nor the city have provided suitable space for a marking room – a location where donated items can be sorted and priced before being put on sale at the retail shop. Karen Eppler, who has been involved with DBFL since its inception said the organization moved to the Carriage House around 1993. Before that it operated out of a vacant classroom in Havens School, Elementary, and then from an unused classroom at Piedmont High. “After that we hauled it all back and used another room at Havens,” she recalled. “I was on the committee to find us a space in Piedmont after the Carriage House,” said Huldah Hodgkinson, who has been the vice president of DBFL for four years. “Conna McCarthy from City Council and Hillary Cooper from the School Board were reps. The school district did offer us spaces, but not the amount we needed. One was a tiny side alley between Driscoll [Playhouse] and Havens.” Dress Best has donated about $100,000 a year to the Piedmont Education Foundation. Since moving to the church at 2501 Harrison St., this has no longer been possible as Piedmonters no longer have a convenient space to donate clothes, shoes, accessories, and household items. “It was disillusioning that the district had the money to construct two new buildings”–. the Alan Harvey Theater and the STEAM Building at Piedmont High – “but had no space for us. Our mission is to support the schools, and this made us feel devalued,” said Hodgkinson. Piedmont School District’s budget for 2022-2023 is over $52 million. Since last week’s arson at the new location (across the street from Whole Foods at 27th & Harrison in Oakland), Hodgkinson said that DBFL’s about 20 volunteers have been even more demoralized. “We don’t have the police support in Oakland that we had in Piedmont. We file a report and that’s all; no one comes. Not to mention the usual urban issues, like people urinating and defecating on our building. The volunteers we rely on don’t feel totally safe working under these conditions, and I believe it’s just a matter of time until someone breaks into the actual building,” she added. The fire completely scorched a 10-foot square storage shed, and charred a donation bin half that size to the point of unusability. Eppler said DBFL board members could not yet provide an estimate for replacement, as they are still discussing cost setbacks with insurance providers. DBFL staff member Beverly Bucci, who has been involved with the organization for 15-20 years, said “when we were at the Carriage House, the donation bin was always full. We’d easily get 10 donators a day. Now it’s more like three to four.” “I’d like to emphasize how close we still are to Piedmont, only two miles,” added staff member Sharon Sanford, who has been involved with DBFL for 20-30 years. “This space sure isn’t an advantage to us,” she said, “especially since we have to make even more room for the bags that would have gone in the burned bins. However, our very large parking lot and dropoff space can be an advantage to Piedmonters.” While DBFL has considered downsizing to only keep their retail store on Piedmont Avenue next door to Piedmont Grocery, this store alone does not have adequate space to store donations, nor a place for dropping off items. For DBFL staff, the future is uncertain. “We’re seriously rethinking whether our business is viable; we can’t continue like this,” said Hodgkinson. “Sustainability – reusing, recycling – is Piedmont’s mission, and it’s crucial to us. We’re asking the community to support us in our mission to help Piedmont schools.” Those interested in donating to DBFL may find a list of acceptable items and make an appointment at dressbestforless.org.

articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 2 is coming to town Sunday, April 23, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in Piedmont Park, and will be a super-sized multicultural festival with many aspects for visitors to experience. Piedmont Food Fest will feature 30 Bay Area food vendors, breweries, and wineries including several Piedmonter-run businesses, including Robert Dorsey Catering, Tea on Piedmont, Bakesum, Mo’s Bakeshop, and Yumbini. This year’s live performances will include Hiiwav music showcase featuring Meaghan Maples and Tyler Reese, Emeryville Taiko, Renegade Opera, LIKHA Pilipino Folk Ensemble, Oakland Samba Revue, and the Han Martial Arts Demo Exhibition. Volunteer slots are now available to assist with check-In, the KidZone carnival, as well as vendor and artist setups. Guests may register for free at www.piedmontfoodfest.org as well as pre-order drink packages, carnival passes, and snackpacks. All registrants who sign up before the event will be eligible to win gift certificates from sponsors Mulberry’s Market and Marielle Hayes Photography.

articles.text: Becker Dashing through a downpour, more than 100 students and parents flooded into Alan Harvey Theatre eager to further uncover one of America’s greatest mysteries – the college admissions process. On Tuesday, March 21, during a heavy rain and windstorm, the Regional Admissions Counselors of California (RACC) hosted a mock admission night for Piedmont students to learn what makes a strong college application. “I’m sure most kids would agree, the whole process of doing your applications can be really hard to understand. I think attending this can help take some of that mystery away,” said Axel Saldanha, a junior at Piedmont High. The attendees were first presented with information about “Lake Washington University”, a fictional college meant to simulate a school that students might apply to. The students then split into groups and reviewed mock applications, deciding which would be accepted, waitlisted, or rejected. “Looking through the applications was really interesting; we got to see the process from the other side, which I think will be helpful,” George Stein. Afterwards tables were displayed with information about colleges for students to look into, including Texas Christian University, University of Arizona, and University of Oregon. “I’m glad I attended. I think the whole event helped bring me closer to the finish line with my college apps,” said Cole Nash. Among the event’s organizers was Arizona College Admissions Counselor Molly Ingram. “I absolutely think the event went well tonight. I was impressed with how many people braved the wind and rain and came out to see how the application process works,” Ingram said. Micah Temple and William Becker are Piedmont High School students and interns with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: In spite of storm, big turnout for Mock Admission Night

articles.text: I was listening to a podcast featuring Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith in which she was discussing the seven different kinds of rest that we need. One really stood out to me: Creative Rest. Her definition of creativity is any time we need to solve a problem. moment of parenting is an act of creativity. How do we get the kids out of the house in the morning when they are moving as slow as turtles? How can we get the siblings to stop arguing over who gets to choose the show to watch during screen time? How do we convince an unwilling child to engage in homework that is hard? All of these problems require creativity in order to solve them, and as parents we are in a constant state of creative thinking. Dr. Dalton-Smith recommends that those of us who are in creative thinking mode all day every day need a rest from that kind of work and that we can find that rest through viewing beauty. That could be through seeing art in an art gallery, going to see live theatre, listening to music or spending time in nature. I realized that, in my life, pre-pandemic, I engaged in a lot of these activities – exploring a new exhibit at a museum, watching musicals and plays, going to live concerts – but all of these activities came to an abrupt halt when the Covid shutdown started. Instead, I drastically increased my time in nature. Like so many others, taking walks, going on hikes, camping, cross country skiing all became a lifeline for me. It wasn’t until I heard this podcast that I realized that being outdoors – in the mountains, at the beach, observing wildflowers – had taken on a critical new dimension, both physical and spiritual. Now that the arts and culture sector has opened again, I am seeing shows again – and it feels amazing. But I am still in nature whenever possible, and I have a newfound appreciation for the creativity and beauty of nature. • The wind in the trees is a symphony. • The sunset is a glorious painting. • Two squirrels arguing over an acorn is theater. • The movement of the waves as they crash on the shore is modern dance. As we move into the spring and summer, I want to encourage all parents to take the Creative Rest we need. Find the beautiful things that inspire you. Go see the shows and enjoy the exquisite nature all around us. It might just give your depleted system the rest it needs. Nina Meehan is a Creativity Consultant and Speaker and founder of Bay Area Children’s Theater. Find out more information about her work at gocreate. zone.
articles.title: Finding Creative Rest in a busy world

articles.text: “Empathy. It’s really rooted in empathy” nods 8th grader Sophia Harris. Sophia, along with Lily Riley, Zoe Snyder, Camille Edesess and Nora Taggart have organized and planned a ceremony called the Council of All Beings for five 6th grade Green Team wheel rotations. But wait. What is the council of all beings anyway? Developed in 1985 by Joanna Macy, the council is a communal gathering where participants dress up as animals and have a conversation with humans as if they were the animals. The goal of this ritual is to feel what animals go through and to recognize our impact on the ecosystem. This school year Piedmont Middle School has adapted the council for its 6th graders, teaching them the importance of empathy and seeing how humans are not superior and that all animals – including humans – are all connected. The council consists of 8th graders who play humans asking the animals three questions: Who are you and what do you contribute to the ecosystem? What message do you want to give the humans? What gift would you give the humans? After all the questions were answered the students took off their masks and threw them into the middle of the circle. After the ceremony, I had the wonderful opportunity to speak to some 6th graders about why they felt the Council was an important and impactful experience. Elly Mak, who represented a Siberian tiger said, “To me, the council is all about noticing what is wrong and what we can do to change.” On the other hand, Aava Lokre, who represented a panda, noted that it was more about “feeling interconnected and giving animals a voice”. Naiomi Jerez stated, “We need to see things from a different perspective and overall, feel a sense of empathy”. Empathy. Empathy is the theme, and the purpose of the council – and what it all comes back to. Samantha Pell is a seventh grade intern with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Council of All Beings launched at middle school

articles.text: Playing lacrosse in a hurricane is no joke During the afternoon of Tuesday March 21, one of the worst rainstorms on record hit the state of California. It was so intense that trees fell, the power went out, and flooding was widespread. Any rational person would look outside and come to the conclusion that any planned outdoor activity could wait. Any activity that required leaving the house should have been put on hold. Yet for reasons still unknown the Bentley girls’ lacrosse team chose not to reschedule or forfeit. Having an all-weather field means to some that you play regardless of weather, unless there is lighting. That Tuesday there was everything: hurricane-strength wind gusts, near-freezing temperatures, rain pouring as if from a bucket, but no lightning. Our team was scheduled to play International High School from San Francisco, who were driving to Lafayette. While players were changing into uniforms, there wasn’t one person who didn’t utter the words, “I don’t want to play right now.” And rightfully so. The rain picked up and so did the wind. Most of the players had some sort of extra layer on – sweatshirt, sweatpants or both. it was the one day I didn’t have my sweats at a game, so I slipped a jacket underneath my uniform for some semblance of warmth. As we ran onto the field, the rain picked up once more. The players were more than happy to start warm-ups – anything to get our blood pumping. my fingers started to freeze, and my lacrosse stick became extremely slippery and passes became harder. Our team wanted to get a win and get off the field and into the warm comfort of our homes, but the game hadn’t even started yet. Our coach gathered us for a team huddle, but the morale was rock bottom. When the coach assured us this was better weather than in Scotland (where he once coached), no one laughed. pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 5, 2023 9 Council of All Beings launched at middle school By Samantha R. Pell “Empathy. It’s really rooted in empathy” nods 8th grader Sophia Harris. Sophia, along with Lily Riley, Zoe Snyder, Camille Edesess and Nora Taggart have organized and planned a ceremony called the Council of All Beings for five 6th grade Green Team wheel rotations. But wait. What is the council of all beings anyway? Developed in 1985 by Joanna Macy, the council is a communal gathering where participants dress up as animals and have a conversation with humans as if they were the animals. The goal of this ritual is to feel what animals go through and to recognize our impact on the ecosystem. This school year Piedmont Middle School has adapted the council for its 6th graders, teaching them the importance of empathy and seeing how humans are not superior and that all animals – including humans – are all connected. The council consists of 8th graders who play humans asking the animals three questions: Who are you and what do you contribute to the ecosystem? What message do you want to give the humans? What gift would you give the humans? After all the questions were answered the students took off their masks and threw them into the middle of the circle. After the ceremony, I had the wonderful opportunity to speak to some 6th graders about why they felt the Council was an important and impactful experience. Elly Mak, who represented a Siberian tiger said, “To me, the council is all about noticing what is wrong and what we can do to change.” On the other hand, Aava Lokre, who represented a panda, noted that it was more about “feeling interconnected and giving animals a voice”. Naiomi Jerez stated, “We need to see things from a different perspective and overall, feel a sense of empathy”. Empathy. Empathy is the theme, and the purpose of the council – and what it all comes back to. Samantha Pell is a seventh grade intern with the Piedmont Post. articles.text: Last weekend a total of 37 students from Highlander Robotics traveled to the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Monterey Bay Regional Tournament with their robot “Paddo the Frog”. They placed second and earned a place at the World Championship in two weeks in Houston. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot must be built for each season and competitions begin 6 weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall scored points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals, as well as balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station”. During regional competitions, teams play up to 12 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners. The highest individually ranked eight teams then become alliance captains and draft two others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoffs and best-of-three finals. After the first day of qualifying rounds in Monterey, the Highlanders had a 6-2 record and in fifth place of 36 behind 2019 World Champion MadTown Robotics from Madera, last year’s World Championship Roebling Division Finalist BREAD Robotics from Redwood City, 2009 World Champion Spartan Robotics from Mountain View, and Duncan Dynamics from Fresno. Highlander Robotics had shown they could keep up. They ranked third in points overall and in one round had won nearly unassisted after one alliance partners was carried off the field before the match began. They were guaranteed to have the option to be an alliance captain if they stayed in fifth through their last three quals, but their best path to Worlds would be as a first pick. Invitations to the World Championship are earned by the winning alliance of a regional tournament as well as by winners of FIRST’s two most prestigious judged awards, Engineering, Inspiration, and Impact. “[Top ranked] MadTown qualified in Fresno and was favored to win at Monterey, likely in an alliance with the #2 team, BREAD. If that happened they would generate a wildcard” said Rui de Figueiredo, the Highlander’s Ava Grochowski passes a cone to the Highlanders Robot Paddo the Frog. Scouting and Strategy mentor. “Spartan, who we expected to be the captain of the second seed alliance, had won the San Francisco Regional so any wildcard would skip them.” This meant that Rookie All Star, if awarded, was the only thing standing in the way of sending the Spartan’s first pick to Worlds should they make Pit crew members (left to right) Helena Young, Beck Peterson, and Reece Beck wait for a robot inspector to qualify Paddo as ready to compete. Paddo scores by placing a cone on the Charged Up grid. Paddo (8033) scores by climbing the see-saw-like Charging Station. finals. “So we waited and hoped everything went right”, said de Figueiredo. Things started well the next morning as the Highlanders decisively won their last three qualification rounds. In the second round of the series, they found themselves on an alliance with Spartan Robotics and had an opportunity to audition the partnership. The result, 170-92, left the team hopeful. “We just work really well together” said Captain Alex Ware. Shortly after, Spartan confirmed their intention to draft the Highlanders. The second seed alliance of Spartan Robotics, Highlander Robotics, and The Apes of Wrath from San Jose went 3-1 in the double elimination playoffs, only losing to the first seed alliance of MadTown, BREAD, and Unipards from Taipei. In the best of three finals, the MadTown lead alliance won in two high intensity rounds 184- 152 and 158-150. As finalists, the only thing that would prevent MadTown’s wildcard going to the Highlanders would be a Rookie All Star. “Then I saw the award on the presenter’s table” said Ware. Rookie team The Mechanical Magicians from Newark had earned the wildcard to Houston. “It was clearly well deserved, but hard not to feel disappointed” he added. Very few paths to Worlds remained. The Highlanders could win Engineering Inspiration or Impact themselves and qualify directly or an additional wildcard could be generated if BREAD or Unipards won. So the team waited and hoped as the awards were announced. Teams can win only one judged award per competition, so any other award would eliminate a possibility. The Highlanders won the Imagery Award, which celebrates attractiveness in engineering and outstanding visual aesthetic integration of machine and team appearance. In particular, the judges recognized the Highlanders rebrand, led by Ava Grochowski, Chloe Kessinger, and Jessica Liu, which sought to maintain a connection to Piedmont while being more inclusive to non-PHS students. BREAD won the Engineering Excellence award. Unipards won Engineering Inspiration, triggering a second wildcard and sending Highlander Robotics back to Houston. “[It was a] rush of emotions. All the hard work had finally paid off.” said Ware. Fundraiser before Worlds The Highlanders are now fundraising to pay the $5000 registration fee, costs to ship the robot and pit, and financial aid for students. Community members can help by making a donation at: frc8033.com. Paddo the Frog was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Matteo Scanu and supported by drive coach Alex Ware, technician Nate Hart, and human player Ava Grochowski. Helena Young and Peter Stokes led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 17 full contact matches with turnarounds as quick as 30 minutes. Jasper Tripp led scouting and strategy operations. Lewy Seiden led a team of 5 ambassadors who fielded questions, built connections with other teams, and represented the team to FIRST Judges. articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Palo Alto on Saturday, April 1, for the prestigious and highly competitive Stanford Invitational The Highlanders competed in two relays and four individual events this year. “This was particularly fun as competitors from all over the West Coast and beyond drove and flew in to compete in front of college coaches, athletes, and Stanford alumni. We had some great performances,” said first year PHS head coach Pouyan Assadi. In a strong outing for Parker Long, the senior finished third of 26 runners in the 800- meter run with a blazing time of 1:53.77, a half-second from matching his personal best set at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. “For this meet he got caught up at the beginning but was able to make his way to the front. He has the skills and motivation to continue on this incredible trajectory, and if we do our part as coaches, he’ll take the leap,” said Assadi. It was also a good day for classmate Christian Taylor, who placed 8th in a field of 26 runners in the 1600 with a personal record time of 4:15.07, topping his previous best by 3.6 seconds set at the Dublin Distance event. Taylor was also 21st in the 800 with a time of 2:00.14. Taylor’s time in the 1600 makes him the school’s third fastest runner of all time, .15 behind Tom Phelps’ time of 4:14.92 in 2001 and .30 back of Jack Stein’s 4:14.77 performance last year. “Christian is a true leader,” said Assadi. Also competing was Spencer Sorensen-Wald in the 400 meter hurdles, finishing 11th of 18 in 59.85. Piedmont’s girls’ 4x100 relay team of Miranda Liu, Ella Yasar, Darcy Mckee, and Breah Bell finished with a time of 51.24, and the boys’ 4x400m relay team of Sorenson-Wald, Long, Shelby, and Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai placed 18th with a time of 3:32.54. “The girls 4x100 are already competing against the best, and we’ve only gotten a small glimpse of what they’re truly capable of,’ said Assadi. articles.text: Dragons set stage for victory with early lead over Spartans An early lead helped the Piedmont Dragons defeat the Piedmont Spartans 11-4 on Sunday, April 2, at Humphries Field in the 2nd annual Piedmont Pony City Baseball Championship. The baseball teams are comprised of local seventh and eighth graders. Base hits by Mateo Quintero and Milo Chipman brought in three runs and keyed a big six-run second inning. Quintero led the Dragons with two hits and three RBIs. Chase Knapp reached base three times. Mateo Long and Knapp each scored twice. Long and Derek Lee each had three stolen bases as the Dragons stole a total of 20 bases. The Spartans racked up nine hits on the day. John Bunje and Griffin Guidi each managed multiple hits. Bunje went 3-for-3 at the plate to lead the Spartans, while Sammy Ragones hit an RBI double to deep left field to score the first run of the game. The big story of the game was the Dragon defense led by a rare complete game from starting pitcher Derek Lee, who was named tournament MVP. He allowed just four runs over seven innings, striking out four while walking only two. Evan Ma caught all seven innings, and the Lee-Ma battery held the Spartans to just two stolen bases. All players contributed to an errorfree performance by the Dragon defense, with key contributions by Theo Barber at shortstop and Russel Pan at first base. Special thanks to Commissioners Dave Ragones and Kim Hunter who conceived the City Championship. The Dragons also won last year’s Championship by defeating the Spartans in the inaugural edition. Both Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation teams compete in the East Bay Pony Premier League with teams from Moraga, Orinda, and Lafayette. The Spartans are currently in first place with a record of 5-1, while the Dragons evened their season mark to 3-3 with the Championship win. The Piedmont Dragons team won the Piedmont Pony Baseball Championship.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California celebrates Earth Day this Friday, April 7. The free family-friendly event begins at 5 p.m. in the museum’s courtyard and garden. Guests will discover the unique flora and foliage of the Oak, Chaparral, and Redwood forest regions of California. Young museum goers can create art inspired by California’s native plants and learn about Earth Day events offered in the Bay Area this month. Special guest, Stomper, the Oakland A’s mascot, will be in attendance. From 6 p.m. to 7 p.m., educator Bowen Lyam Lee will read Stories for a Healthy Planet in the garden. Lee is a fifth generation Chinese American born and raised in Oakland, and has been a teacher for 36 years, incorporating storytelling into all aspects of teaching. DJ Benet will be playing in the Amphitheater from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. This event is part of the museum’s Friday Nights series, where food trucks, live music and art-inspired activities are available. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid-earth-day/.

articles.text: Botanist-guided classes this week The Filoli Garden House Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside will host botanical bouquet workshops now through April 7 to celebrate its spring blooms. The garden’s veteran staff will guide you through a bouquet-making session featuring the estate’s well-prized flowers. Filoli is home to 16 acres of formal gardening grounds and a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. The most fertile and popular flowers during March are Camellias, Magnolias, Irises, and Wisteria. In April, the historic gardens will welcome a bloom of roses and Lavender. The workshop is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. Light refreshments and wine are provided with registration purchase. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ flora-party/ or call (650) 364- 8300 to purchase tickets. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside.
articles.title: Mix the perfect bouquet with Filoli staff

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is currently performing Cinderella onstage through April 8. Choreographer Christopher Wheeldon transforms the classic fairytale set to Sergei Prokofiev’s score with mesmerizing visual effects and stunning costume design by Tony Award-winning designer Julian Crouch. Included in this production is San Francisco-native puppeteer Basil Twist, who creates a tree that grows from the princess’s tears at the end of Act I. Cinderella is a co-production of Dutch National Ballet, and first premiered at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House in 2013. Educator Appreciation Day: April 7 San Francisco Ballet will host an Educator Appreciation Day this Friday, April 7, welcoming teachers, paraprofessionals, school staff, administrators, and teaching artists from schools across the Bay Area to view the production. Cinderella runs approximately 2 hours and 30 minutes including two intermissions. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ cinderella/, or call the box office at 415-865-2000.
articles.title: SF Ballet performing Cinderella through April 8

articles.text: How can so much exuberance emanate from one of the most depressing large-scale symphonies ever written? Easy. You put a beloved ex-maestro like Michael Tilson Thomas back on the podium. Upon entry, the revered 78-yearold conductor got a standing ovation from the near-sell-out crowd. And at the end, the fired-up patrons accorded the S.F. Symphony and him an inordinately rare six-minute ovation. Gustav Mahler (1860-1911) himself would never have believed it for the deeply aggrieved Sixth Symphony of 1904, which had left the ultra-emotional composer sobbing uncontrollably on first hearing. Here was the ultimate late romantic, carried away by his own music – so searing in its impact, he could not contain his emotions. Analysis from this (distant) vantage-point seat suggests it all dealt with premonitions of death. His heart was never fully sound, presaging his demise at age 50. The finale’s sledge-hammer blows on a resonant wood box, executed by percussionist Jacob Nissly with a Donner-sized sledge from the balcony a full floor higher than the stage, are unique in music as such premonitions, even more so than the death-rattle bass trill interrupting the melody of the Schubert Piano Sonata in B Flat Major’s opening (that being the speculation by pianist Andras Schiff). We have to thank Mahler’s unquenchable work ethic, and presumably the Almighty, that he was around to write three-plus additional symphonies, along with vocal works. But none of the later ones resonated with such tragedy as the music of the Sixth. Still, it’s a thoroughly engrossing, mammoth-scale opus whose complexity and giant-sized orchestra draws you along with it – passionate despair be damned. The Sixth is a multi-dimensional wonderworld full of trapdoors. The long opening movement is a dour military march toward some lemming-like goal. The Scherzo has another funeral march in minor with big brass gestures and snare drums. Only the appearance of the sweet-tender Ländler (Austrian waltz-predecessor) mitigates among the abrupt gearshifts, some of them on tiptoe. Finally the slow movement arrives with its eight (!) French horns and a woodwind chorale, all a genteel, spacey escape in the midst of this voyage of heavenly length. The multitude of emotions is like itself – only that Mahler suffered the extremes more than perhaps anyone. The boisterous finale offers tumult via the ominous boxsmasher, plus horns playing bells-up in a raw sound mode. The frenzy subsides now and then, enabling cowbells to sound out offstage. Currents and crosscurrents endure until a brassy ending, still with strings bowing away tirelessly, comes as you had never dared possible, with fulfillment and a measure of relief. The performance was inspiring. Most notable is that all the augmented sections, like four clarinets, two harps, six trumpets, etc. – coalesced into a coherent whole without loose ends. This was an achievement of which MTT could be proud into his retirement days – if they ever come. MUSIC NOTES MTT’s return to action has come this season with much cheering, as only optimists could have predicted given his precarious brain-cancer operation (glioblastoma) of a year ago. Three cheers for the unsung tuba: At the end of the March 30 concert, MTT accorded the first of the orchestral bows to Jeffrey Anderson, the tuba principal who too often is taken for granted. San Francisco Symphony with M.D. Laureate MTT in Mahler’s Symphony No. 6, March 30-April 1. Davies Hall. S.F. articles.text: Fire of Love, a documentary by Piedmont High School alumnus Sara Dosa, class of 2000, was nominated for an Oscar this year. The film follows the life of husband and wife, Maurice and Katia Krafft, who studied volcanoes throughout the world and captured the most intense interior photos on record. Dosa premiered the film at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival, where it was one of five films selected in the documentary category. Following the festival it was purchased for national distribution in theaters by National Geographic Documentary Films, a worldwide rights deal valued at a mid-seven-figure deal. Dosa is an Indie Spirit Award-nominated director and Peabody Award-winning producer, whose film credits include Audrie & Daisy, available on at-home streaming service Netflix, The Seer and Unseen, and The Last Season. Fire of Love, Dosa’s documentary chronicling the work of Maurice and Katia Krafft, French husband-wife volcanologists, opened the Sundance Film A scene from documentary Fire of Love, which recently was a nominee for an Academy Award Documentary film director and producer Sara Dosa, a Piedmont native Festival on January 20. The film contains over 20 years of archival footage and dramatic shots of active volcanoes and explosions beginning in 1966. The Krafft couple traveled to volcanic locations in Zaire, Iceland, the Americas and Japan, capturing then-unseen footage of seismic, tectonic eruptions. Under Dosa’s direction, the team behind Fire of Love weaved the footage together to tell the couple’s love story, The Kraffts spent decades collecting data mere feet away from danger. In 1991 they were killed capturing an explosion on Japan’s Mount Unzen. Their legacy included some of the most dramatic footage humans may ever be able to capture. “I like to think of it as a love triangle. Maurice and Katia were obviously the love story that drove [the narrative], but you also have the volcanoes they chased. In a way they were both in love with this important work they did,” Dosa said. T he docu ment a r y was reviewed favorably in both the New York Times and the San Francisco Chronicle. A.O. Scott, co-chief film critic for the New York Times, noted the exceptional cinematography of the film. “The sheer existence of these photos is mind-boggling when you think about how close the people with the cameras must have been to the lava and the smoke,” said Scott. As director, Dosa had her hand in every stage of the film, including in the documentary’s clever use of animation and in writing the copy provided to Miranda July, author and independent film screenwriter, who narrates the film. Dosa said she consulted with colleagues of the Kraffts when considering what story she wanted to tell - but that the bulk of the narration comes directly from the footage the couple captured, and the Kraffts’ own notes, speeches and published works. National Geographic Films released Fire of Love on July 6, 2022. Dosa’s documentary is showing at Alamo Drafthouse Cinema, New Mission, and AMC Kabuki 8 theatre in San Francisco. To find a theater near you where the film is playing and to stream online, visit: https://films.nationalgeographic.com/fire-of-love.

articles.text: Guillermo del Toro’s reimagined Pinocchio, based on the classic Carlo Collodi’s children’s book written in 1883, won an Oscar for Best Animated Feature at this year’s 2003 Academy Awards. But parents should know that this stop-motion version, while immensely creative, is not your grandfather’s Pinocchio. Disney or Pixar it’s not. The reframed story opens by introducing the audience to Geppetto (David Bradley), an elderly Italian woodcarver, and his much-adored young son Carlo. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pinecone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pinecone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the bombers has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned, knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding the boy in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pinecone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has now become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that his grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But there does appear in the early dawn, while Geppetto sleeps, a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him and the villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by del Toro and Mark Gustafsen, A stop-motion animation. Voiced by Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradley. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Netflix.

But parents should know that this stop-motion version, while immensely creative, is not your grandfather’s Pinocchio. Disney or Pixar it’s not. The reframed story opens by introducing the audience to Geppetto (David Bradley), an elderly Italian woodcarver, and his much-adored young son Carlo. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pinecone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pinecone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the bombers has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned, knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding the boy in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pinecone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has now become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that his grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But there does appear in the early dawn, while Geppetto sleeps, a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him and the villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by del Toro and Mark Gustafsen, A stop-motion animation. Voiced by Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradley. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Springtime means brunch time for many of us. And finally, we are slated for some dry and sunny days to gather with family and friends. I often make a frittata for our Sunday brunch. It’s usually in a 12-inch skillet to savor leftovers the next day. I’ve modified a springtime favorite to bake in muffin tins for individual servings, ideal for entertaining and your brunch spread. Advance notes: It’s important to liberally grease each muffin cup, even if for “nonstick” pans. If well buttered or oiled, the muffins are removed easily. Omit this if using parchment liners. I add the salmon, asparagus pieces (saving the tips for topping), crumbled cheese and chives into the egg mixture; just as I do for a large frittata. For mini-frittatas, carefully fill each cup with about the same amounts of everything in each. If you want to be more precise, layer the fillings before adding the egg mix as follows: asparagus pieces, salmon pieces, crumbled cheese and lastly chives on top. Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Serves 12 INGREDIENTS • 10 large eggs • 1/2 cup whole milk • 4 ounces cold smoked, sliced sockeye salmon • 12 stalks asparagus, about the diameter of a pencil. • 2.5 ounces goat cheese, crumbled (about 1/3 cup) • 1/4 cup fresh chives, cut into 1/4-inch lengths • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste • 2 teaspoons olive oil, extra-virgin • Vegetable oil spray or butter for greasing the muffin tins. Omit if using parchment liners. INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 12-cup muffin pan by liberally greasing each cup or use parchment liners. Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Cut a 1-1/2 inch length of the asparagus tips off, then cut the remaining stalks into 1/2-inch pieces to measure a generous one-half cup of pieces. Heat the 2 teaspoons of olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add all the asparagus pieces and sauté until just tender. Remove from heat and set aside. Separate the asparagus tips from the 1/2-inch pieces, the tips will be used to decorate the tops of each frittata. Cut the smoked salmon into 1/2-inch squares by first cutting the entire piece of adhered sliced salmon in half lengthwise. Stack the two pieces atop each other, then cut in 1/2-inch strips lengthwise. Turn the strips 90-degrees and cut these strips crosswise in 1/2-inch increments. Gently separate the slices. It’s OK if there are a few of the thin slices stick together. Whisk together the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add the salmon, asparagus pieces, cheese, and chives and stir to evenly distribute. (Optional: see the advance note above to layer the filling.) Divide evenly among muffin cups, leaving about 1/4-inch from the rim. Bake for 10 minutes, then remove the muffin pan to place an asparagus tip atop each mini frittata. Return to the oven, continue baking until the frittatas are lightly browned, set in the center, and puffed up. Total baking time is about 18 – 20 minutes. (Their puffy splendor is temporary, as they will fall to about even to the rim upon removal from the oven.) Transfer the muffin pan to a wire rack and cool for 10 minutes. Use a small silicone spatula to loosen around the edges and bottoms of each tin. Remove gently and serve warm.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Louis (Lou) Highman, beloved father, brother, uncle, and friend, passed away on March 23, 2023. Born Louis A. Highman, he was the second of three sons born to Arthur and Edith Arkoff Highman. He grew up in the San Fernando Valley and graduated from Birmingham High School in Van Nuys in 1965. While in high school he was student body vice president, the salutatorian of his senior class, and a champion debater. At age 16, Louis was admitted to Stanford University and graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1969. He obtained a J.D. from Boalt Hall School of Law at the University of California, Berkeley in 1974. Between college and law school, Louis served for two years in the AmeriCorps Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA) program. After law school, he worked as a legal aid attorney for the San Francisco Neighborhood Legal Assistance Foundation before becoming a founding member of Highman, Highman & Ball, an employment and consumer law firm. Louis was a committed and talented advocate, whose legal skills and dedication improved the lives of many individuals. With cases he pursued through the higher courts, Louis helped establish precedents that continue to bolster the rights of employees and consumers. Louis enjoyed sharing his professional knowledge and experience with fellow lawyers, students, and the broader public through teaching and television and radio appearances. In 1988, Louis married Shannon Maloney and within a few years they were a family of four with two daughters, Alice and Molly. As a young family, they shared many happy times traveling, enjoying new adventures, and visiting family and friends. Louis was devoted to Shannon. Her death in 2009 was a hard Louis Highman passed away on March 23. blow, but Louis put his family ahead of his own loss. The happiness, well-being, and education of Alice and Molly became his priority. Being a father was his most treasured job and he excelled at it. Louis eagerly shared with his daughters his experiences, interests, and talents, including music, language, travel, and a lifelong love for France, which he developed during a college semester abroad in Tours, France. He was a patient and encouraging coach for the girls’ soccer and softball teams, and later he lent his considerable experience to their high school mock trial team. Louis’ sense of adventure, intellectual curiosity, and humor were matched only by his profound kindness, gentleness, and idealism. He will be dearly missed by his daughters, brothers Mark (Phyllis) and Bruce (Justine), nieces, nephews, cousins, and many (many) friends. A funeral service was held on March 27, 2023 at Mountain View Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that memorial donations be made to the American Civil Liberties Union or another organization that honors Louis’ values and memory.

She was named City Manager of nearby Brawley where she worked for nine years, “collaborating with staff to operationalize a new fire station, establishing a new Emergency Operations Center, and renovating multiple high utilization parks, in partnership with community groups and engaged residents.” After being named Assistant City Manager of Antioch in 2020, she and her husband moved there. “Because I hadn’t been in a setting with a very large population before,” she said, “I thought it was important to add to my experience from a different position. Senior Stitch Lawrence imitated the anti-social “Go-Away Bird;” freshman Theo Ferguson, made a splash with his blue flippers as the Blue Footed Booby seabird; and the California Gull, by freshman Isabelle Myers, shed a new light on sandwich-stealing seagulls. The winners were chosen by a panel of five judges, including PHS English teacher Jamieson Mockel, Vice Principal Irma Muñoz, PHS alum Joe Fendel, and celebrity judges Rosemary Orozco and Michael Poryes. Orozco is an Emmy AwardWinning meteorologist on KTVU. Poryes, a 1973 PHS alum, produced Disney Channel hits “Hanna Montana,” “That’s so Raven” and “Life with Boys”. The PHS dance team gave a graceful performance to begin the show, Emcee Daniel Banin, a junior, cracked birding jokes in between acts, and the PHS Jazz Quartet played while the judges deliberated. This year’s contest added a new tradition, “The Great Squawk,” with past Bird Calling participants joining the competitors on stage for one final combined call. The Bird Calling Contest originated in 1963, with students attempting bird calls in the classroom of science and biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck. It was instantly popular and had to be moved to the school auditorium the following year. But as the show continues after five decades and a pandemic, the contest has become anything but regular. Past winners were invited on ‘The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson,’ and ‘Late Night with David Letterman.’ In 2022, 2015 Bird Calling winner, Maya Guzdar, showed off her call as an audience member on “The Daily Show with Trever Noah.” “As a ‘new kid,’ the silly spirit of the Bird Calling Contest helped me feel at home in Piedmont,” said Guzdar, “The contest is important, not only for its historical legacy, but in carrying forward that lightness and ‘I can make fun of myself’ attitude for Piedmont. I’m so happy that the contest is back. Let’s work as a community to keep it going.” Sohrab “Seb” Ford is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post. She was named City Manager of nearby Brawley where she worked for nine years, “collaborating with staff to operationalize a new fire station, establishing a new Emergency Operations Center, and renovating multiple high utilization parks, in partnership with community groups and engaged residents.” After being named Assistant City Manager of Antioch in 2020, she and her husband moved there. “Because I hadn’t been in a setting with a very large population before,” she said, “I thought it was important to add to my experience from a different position. It helped me remember that no matter the size of the city, so many issues with regard to delivering public services, maintaining infrastructure, and planning for future growth within certain financial constraints are similar.” After two years with Antioch, where she led “initiatives to design a bridge housing program for unsheltered residents and a 24-hour, 365-day community crisis intervention team,” Bayon Moore “became interested in finding an involved community where I could serve in the lead position and work directly with the Council and city staff.” Upon hearing of the job opening in Piedmont, she was struck by the city’s high level of community engagement and “the commitment of its local leaders to the democratic process. Productive dialogue never ends up the way you expect it to, yet there’s always solid decision-making as an outcome.” “Piedmont is a built-out community of 1.7 square miles … The best part is that the size allows for local government to be so in tune with residents and with opportunities to develop as a community,” she said. Bayon Moore has been working with retiring City Administrator Sara Lillevand for a twoweek transitional period leading up to her first day. “I am excited to get up to speed with the pool project and build ongoing feedback with the community,’ she added.
